Remember this: Driver/Sales Workers deliver goods and sell them, while delivery drivers only transport them. One sells; the other transports.

It is a poor fit for people who dislike travel, cannot start conversations with store owners, or cannot tolerate outdoor work in sun and rain. The job is field-based every day and requires resilience.
A common path is to start in delivery, become a Driver/Sales Worker, manage a route independently, take responsibility for a territory, and advance to route supervisor or regional management.

This career suits people who can drive, communicate naturally with local customers, and confidently promote products. If you measure success by turning deliveries into repeat orders, you can build a stable career here.

Driver/Sales Workers deliver and sell products along fixed routes. They maintain shelf displays, manage replenishment and payment collection, and build local customer and distribution-channel relationships.

paragraphs: In the morning, Driver/Sales Workers load and count goods before visiting the first store to replenish stock and make sales. At midday, they discuss sell-through with store owners and promote new products. In the afternoon, they complete remaining stops, organize shelves, and collect payments. Before returning, they reconcile orders and prepare the next day's route.

In one sentence: they drive and sell. The work includes delivery, shelf organization, replenishment recommendations, payment collection, new-account development, and customer relationship management. It combines physical travel with sales communication at the front line of distribution.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 451,500 Driver/Sales Workers were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to rise to 491,300 by 2034, a net increase of about 39,800 jobs, with about 51,300 openings each year. Median annual pay was about $37,100 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace Driver/Sales Workers, but it will reduce route-planning work. Navigation and replenishment systems accelerate routing and inventory tasks. Workers who only deliver face the most pressure, while those who can sell and manage accounts become more valuable.

paragraphs: The greatest career risk is e-commerce combined with direct distribution. Systems absorb standard delivery work, while workers with sales skills are more secure.

The main job risks are e-commerce and direct distribution, not AI alone. Systems automate some replenishment, while fuel prices and road conditions affect income. Local customer relationships still require people.

No matter how intelligent systems become, Driver/Sales Workers still visit stores to decide replenishment, create repeat purchases, organize products, and collect payments. Distribution channels cannot fully remove people from these tasks.
In short, the future shortage is not people who can drive, but Driver/Sales Workers who can sell, develop retail locations, and reconcile accounts accurately.
